source_text:
Haec sunt, inquit, salubria uerba ex perenni ac uiuo fonte; quae qui audierit et isdem primum crediderit, deinde, quae insinuant. custodierit, numquam erit morti obnoxius, uerum aeterna et gloriosa uita fruetur. nam profecto beatus est iudicandus, qui hac diuina instructus cognitione fuerit, per quam liberatus in sempiterna uita permanebit. et haec, ut uidetis, pollicitatio est, nondum exhibitio ueritatis: et uos quoque animaduertere facillime potestis isto uelamine quoslibet errores fucari posse, ut inperitorum animis per ornatam ianuam latenter inrepant. si enim diceret: haec sunt pestifera uerba ex uenenoso fonte; quae qui audierit et isdem primum crediderit, deinde. quae insinuant, custodierit, numquam erit uitae restituendus, uerum poenali et aerumnosa morte adficietur — nam profecto miser est iudicandus, qui hac inferna inplicatus inperitia fuerit. per quam demersus in sempiternis cruciatibus permanebit —: si ergo hoc diceret, uerum diceret, sed libro huic nom solum nullum conciliaret lectorem, sed omnes, quorum in manus incidisset, in maxima odia concitaret. quamobrem ad consequentia transeamus nec nos ista decipiant, quae possunt esse bonis et malis, doctis et indoctis uerba communia. quid ergo sequitur?
Pax. inquit, dei inuisibilis et ueritatis notitia sit cum fratribus sanctis et carissimis, qui mandatis caelestibus credunt pariter atque deseruiunt. ita sit, ut dicit. nam et ista benigna et acceptissima optatio est. tantum meminerimus haec et a bonis doctoribus et a deceptoribus posse dici. itaque si nulla nisi talia diceret, omnibus legendum et amplectendum esse concederem. nec illa, quae ad hoc sequuntur, inprobauerim; adiungit enim: sed et dextera luminis tueatur et eripiat uos ab omni incursione maligna et a laqueis mundi. et omnino quicquid in huius epistulae principio scriptum est, donec ueniatur ad causam, nolo reprehendere, ne in rebus minoribus multum operis consumatur. iam ergo euidentissimam pollicitationem hominis uideamus.
thought_title: Mani's opening promises and blessings are common to truth and deceit
orientation: Augustine has just entered the text of Mani's Fundamental Letter and now quotes its opening promises and blessing, then shows that such words could be spoken by either good teachers or deceivers.
pass_a_gloss: These are, he says, health-bringing words from a perennial and living fountain; he who will have heard them and first will have believed these same things, then will have kept the things which they instill, will never be liable to death, but will enjoy eternal and glorious life. For surely he is to be judged blessed who will have been instructed by this divine knowledge, through which, having been freed, he will remain in everlasting life. And these things, as you see, are a promise, not yet an exhibition of the truth: and you too can very easily notice that under this veil any errors whatsoever can be colored over, so that they may creep in secretly into the minds of the inexperienced through an adorned doorway. For if he were to say: these are pestilential words from a poisonous fountain; he who will have heard them and first will have believed these same things, then will have kept the things which they instill, will never be restored to life, but will be afflicted with a penal and wretched death — for surely he is to be judged miserable who will have been entangled in this infernal ignorance, through which, having been plunged down, he will remain in everlasting torments —: if therefore he were to say this, he would say the truth, but he would win for this book not only no reader, but would stir up all those into whose hands it had fallen into the greatest hatred. For this reason let us pass to what follows, and let not those things deceive us, which can be words common to good and bad, learned and unlearned. What therefore follows? Peace, he says, of the invisible God and knowledge of the truth be with the holy and dearest brothers, who believe the heavenly commands and equally serve them. So be it, as he says. For this is also a kind and most acceptable wish. Only let us remember that these things can be said both by good teachers and by deceivers. Therefore if he were to say nothing except such things, I would grant that it should be read and embraced by all. Nor would I disapprove those things which follow to this point; for he adds: but also may the right hand of light guard you and snatch you away from every malignant assault and from the snares of the world. And altogether whatever is written in the beginning of this letter, until one comes to the matter, I do not wish to find fault with, lest much labor be consumed in smaller matters. Now therefore let us look at the most evident promise of the man.

choices.why: Keeps the literal force of salubria as bringing health, matching the medical metaphor of the fountain.

choices.english: from a perennial and living fountain
choices.why: Literal rendering of both adjectives; perennis means ever-flowing, uiuus means living, both describing the source.
rejected: from an eternal and living spring
from a perpetual and living source

choices.why: Obnoxius means exposed or liable to; keeps the legal sense of being subject to death.
Fucari is from fucus, dye or paint; the metaphor is of covering errors with cosmetic color, so 'colored over' preserves the image.
Ornata means decorated or adorned; ianua is a door or entrance, continuing the image of a decorated entrance through which errors creep in.
Literal rendering of dextera luminis; 'light' is the glossary term for the land of light, and dextera is the right hand as a protecting power.

pass_b_english: “These,” Mani says, “are health-bringing words from a perennial and living fountain. Whoever hears them and first believes them, and then keeps what they instill, will never be liable to death, but will enjoy eternal and glorious life. For surely the one who has been instructed in this divine knowledge, through which he is set free and will remain in everlasting life, must be judged blessed.” And this, as you see, is a promise, not yet an exhibition of the truth. You too can very easily notice that under this veil any errors at all can be colored over, so that they creep secretly into the minds of the inexperienced through an adorned doorway. If he had said, “These are pestilential words from a poisonous fountain; whoever hears them and first believes them, and then keeps what they instill, will never be restored to life, but will be struck with a penal and wretched death—for surely the one who has been entangled in this infernal ignorance, through which he is plunged down and will remain in everlasting torments, must be judged miserable”—if he had said this, he would have spoken the truth, but he would not only have won no reader for this book; he would have stirred everyone whose hands it fell into to the greatest hatred. Therefore let us pass on to what follows, and let these things not deceive us, since they can be words common to good and bad, learned and unlearned alike. What follows then?

“May the peace,” he says, “of the invisible God and the knowledge of the truth be with the holy and most dear brothers who alike believe and serve the heavenly commands.” May it be as he says, for this too is a kind and most acceptable wish. Only let us remember that these things can be said by good teachers and by deceivers alike. So if he said nothing but such things, I would grant that he should be read and embraced by all. Nor would I disapprove of what follows next, for he adds: “But may the right hand of light also guard you and rescue you from every evil assault and from the snares of the world.” And in general, whatever is written at the beginning of this letter, until it comes to the matter at hand, I do not wish to criticize, lest much effort be spent on minor points. Let us now look at the man’s most evident promise.

last_rejected.quote: he would not only have won no reader for this book
last_rejected.source_quote: sed libro huic nom solum nullum conciliaret lectorem
last_rejected.why: Source has 'nom' (error for 'non') 'solum' = 'not only'; English 'not only have won no reader' misplaces negation, should be 'would have won not only no reader'.
last_rejected.fix: he would have won not only no reader for this book
last_rejected.ruling: 'not only have won no reader' correctly renders 'non solum nullum conciliaret lectorem'; negation scope is equivalent, not misleading.
